title: The white elephant dream
hook: Queen Maya dreams a white elephant enters her side; the wise men say a great son is coming

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Dhammapada, and camp one closed with twenty-one words. Your line: what you think, you become.
screen: `THE DHAMMAPADA — WHAT YOU THINK, YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: Night, in Kapilavatthu, a city at the foot of the Himalayas. It's the time of a summer festival. Queen Maya, wife of King Suddhodana, has kept the festival well, given gifts, and gone to sleep. She dreams that a white elephant, shining like silver, walks toward her, circles her bed, and enters her side. The Buddha's life story begins here, one scene at a time.
screen: `A CITY BELOW THE MOUNTAINS.` → `A QUEEN DREAMS OF AN ELEPHANT.` → `THE STORY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: In the later tellings, guardian spirits carry Maya up to a high place in the mountains, bathe her in a lake, and lay her on a heavenly couch. A white elephant with six tusks, a white lotus in its trunk, comes down from a golden mountain, trumpets, walks around her three times, and seems to enter her right side. In the morning she tells the king. He calls in the brahmins, the wise men who read signs. Be glad, they say. The queen has conceived, and it's a son. If he stays in the household, he'll be a great king who rules the world. If he leaves it, he'll be a buddha: one who wakes up and removes the veil from the world. Where does this come from? The early discourses describe his conception with wonders, a great light, the earth trembling, but no elephant. The dream comes from later biographies and commentaries, and it's old in its own right: the scene is carved in stone at early Buddhist sites in India, such as Bharhut. Why an elephant? In ancient India a white elephant was a royal treasure, rare and auspicious: strength, gentleness and greatness at once. Across Buddhist Asia the dream is painted on temple walls, and in Thailand and Myanmar the white elephant is still a sign of blessing. Before anyone knows who this child will be, something announces him.
screen: `A LAKE IN THE MOUNTAINS.` · `SIX TUSKS AND A WHITE LOTUS.` · `A KING, OR A BUDDHA.` · `A LATER TELLING, CARVED IN STONE.` · then, large: `SOME THINGS ANNOUNCE THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: From today, the bell gives you two minutes. Sit comfortably and recall a dream that stayed with you, from childhood or from last month: its colors, the place, the feeling when you woke. Don't decide what it meant; some things arrive in us before we understand them, and when the mind wanders, come back to the breath.
White elephant. Queen Maya's dream before the birth: six tusks, a white lotus, and a son who would be a king or a buddha.
Your line: some things announce themselves. Tomorrow, the child arrives, in a garden on the road. That's camp two, day one.

screen: `DAY 22 COUNTS. CAMP TWO BEGINS.` → `TOMORROW: BORN IN A GROVE.`

howItsDone: Buddhists remember Maya's dream in temple murals, carvings and festival plays; in many countries the story is told to children as the first chapter of the Buddha's life, and the white elephant remains a symbol of blessing.

fork.setup: you're King Suddhodana. your queen has dreamed a white elephant entered her side. what do you do?
options: ignore it. it's only a dream.
call the wise men to read it.
send the queen away to rest.
fork.reveal: he calls the brahmins. they tell him to be glad: a son is coming, who will be a great king, or, if he leaves home, a buddha.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fairy-tale opening.
what it means: the first scene of the Buddha's life story, a sign that something great is coming before anyone understands it.

what a scholar hears: the dream is told in the Nidanakatha, the introduction to the Jataka commentary, and in Sanskrit biographies; the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (MN 123) describes the conception's wonders without it. early reliefs at Bharhut show the scene.

chat.says: Why do Buddhists tell a story about an elephant before the Buddha was even born?
options: It was Queen Maya's dream, a sign that a great son was coming.
It was the animal the young prince later rode when he left home.
It comes from the oldest discourses, which describe the elephant in detail.
chat.meaning: Maya dreamed a white elephant entered her side. The wise men read it: a son, a great king or a buddha.

Kapilavatthu.meaning: the Sakyas' city at the foot of the Himalayas

Maya.meaning: the queen who dreamed of the white elephant, the Buddha's mother

Suddhodana.meaning: the king, Maya's husband and the Buddha's father

brahmins.meaning: the wise men who read signs and dreams

Bharhut.meaning: an early Buddhist site in India with stone carvings of the dream

notes: Details of the dream (four guardian kings, Anotatta lake, silver mountain / golden mansion, six tusks, white lotus, circling three times, right side) follow the Nidanakatha as remembered; the script simplifies. Rhys Davids translated the Nidanakatha in Buddhist Birth Stories (1880), but nothing is quoted. Confirm.
The brahmins' interpretation (king or buddha) is from the Nidanakatha; the same prophecy appears again at the naming (day 26). Confirm no clash.
Bharhut relief of Maya's dream: confirm (the trapdoor names Bharhut).
